newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Weizman to Egypt in bid to mend rift.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Weizman to Egypt in bid to mend rift.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing a floodtide of rancour in the Arab world, dispatches President Ezer Weizman to Egypt on Monday in a bid to mend a deep rift at the heart of the Middle East conflict.

Pressed to act swiftly to rescue an Israel-PLO peace deal crippled by gunbattles in the West Bank and Gaza last month, Netanyahu may also hold a U.S.-brokered summit this week with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, officials said.

The outspoken Weizman, a general turned peacemaker whose office is by law largely ceremonial, said his role in Egypt would be to seek to heal "certain splits, which everyone sees, with the largest Arab country, and I think we can find a number of directions for improved relations".
Weizman was a key architect of the landmark 1979 Israel-Egypt peace treaty, the first such agreement between the Jewish state and an Arab country.
Israel's ties with its Arab neighbours, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, and the Palestinians, all but ruptured after Netanyahu's upset victory over Shimon Peres in May elections.

Netanyahu put Arabs on notice that Peres's U.S.-endorsed formula of trading occupied land for peace -- the engine of accelerated peace talks since Peres's slain predecessor Yitzhak Rabin took office in 1992 -- was no longer Israeli policy.

Though Netanyahu has pledged to honour commitments sealed by Nobel Peace laureates Rabin and Peres, his failure thus far to order an already long-delayed troop redeployment from much of the West Bank town of Hebron has taken centre stage in Arab eyes as a test of the tough-talking Israeli leader's intentions.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has said the Hebron issue must be settled before he will agree to meet Netanyahu.
Moreover, Mubarak said a Palestinian backlash to Israel's hawkish positions could force Arafat to "disappear".
"Violence may start," Mubarak told Time magazine. "Not only against Israelis, but against those who support the Israelis."
Mubarak said Egyptians were "furious" over Netanyahu's policies, and some wanted to sever diplomatic ties.

Jordan, not long ago Israel's warmest peace partner, is seen likely to use its strongest language since its 1994 peace treaty when it tells the Jewish state this week that relations hinge on honouring peace accords.

The nosedive in Arab-Israeli relations -- with Israelis suddenly expressing fears of renewed warfare for the first time in years -- has prompted an openly concerned Weizman to assume an activist role rare in Israeli presidential history.

"We are now getting close to the hours of truth, to the hours in which we will need to find a way to solve the problems of living together with the Palestinians ... and the Arab world as a whole," Weizman said in a speech on Sunday as a discomfited Netanyahu looked on grimly.
Earlier this year, Weizman shamed Netanyahu into meeting Arafat, long denounced by the prime minister's Likud party as a "master murderer" and "grand terrorist".
Netanyahu relented in September after Weizman said he would meet Arafat himself if Netanyahu maintained his refusal.
Last week Weizman welcomed Arafat to his seaside home for the Palestinian leader's first public visit to Israel.
Late on Sunday, Israeli and Palestinian officials said Netanyahu might meet Arafat again as early as Wednesday.
They last met in an emergency summit in Washington early this month, following clashes last month in which 60 Arabs and 15 Jews were killed.

Israeli media speculated Mubarak might be disappointed by Netanyahu's failure to order a confidence-building measure to buoy the atmosphere, such as setting a timetable for the pullout from the West Bank flashpoint.
Asked after meeting Netanyahu on Sunday if he had been "equipped" with a message of reconcilation from the prime minister, Weizman told reporters:
"No, no, no. The prime minister has no message such as 'Listen, I'm moving out of Hebron, or redeploying the troops at a certain hour."

Weizman, who is expected to complain to Mubarak about the vilification of Netanyahu in the Egyptian press, said: "I want to sit down with him in a fine manner, and listen to what he has to say, and I have plenty for him to listen to."
